extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, logicians, and readers interested in the philosophy and practice of computer-assisted proofs (proof-assistant users and skeptics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and philosophical criteria for when a computer-derived or computer-checked result counts as a mathematical proof, addressing formalisation, surveyability, legibility, trust in software, and community acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs are convincing
rubrics_metrics.description: “Proofs are convincing.” The paper explains “convincing” as meaning “convincing for mathematicians” and mere acceptance by the mathematical community is sufficient (even if they cannot survey the proof itself).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance by the mathematical community is treated as a legitimate standard of convincingness; machine proofs must persuade mathematicians, not just be mechanically valid. Note the author calls this close to “justification by faith”: mathematicians must believe in proof assistants for a proof to be convincing in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs are surveyable
rubrics_metrics.description: “Proofs are surveyable.” A surveyable proof is one whose main ideas and structure can be inspected by a human (at least in outline) so that the human can be confident in the result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all formal proofs are surveyable; very large/computational proofs (e.g., million-digit facts, largest known primes, Boolean Pythagorean Triples, projective plane of order 10) may be too large to survey. In such cases surveying small arbitrary parts can help establish confidence, and lack of surveyability may be acceptable if the result has few weighty implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs are formalisable
rubrics_metrics.description: “Proofs are formalisable.” A proof should be expressible in a formal logical language and reducible to primitive logical inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof assistants literally formalise proofs; formalisation means both high-level logical expression and reduction to primitive inferences. Formalisability is a widely accepted desideratum and computer-checked proofs typically satisfy it by construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legibility / human-readability of formal proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal proofs should be written to be legible so that humans can read and understand them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some proof languages and systems (e.g., Mizar and Isabelle/HOL’s Isar) are specifically designed for legibility. The author notes that the great majority of formal proofs are not legible in practice, but legible formal proofs can satisfy convincing, surveyable, and formalisable criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: No handwaving; completeness of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Machine proofs must avoid handwaving: they contain detailed, explicit inferences rather than gaps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Machines are typically harder to convince than a knowledgeable mathematician; machine proofs contain excessive detail rather than gaps. This can be a virtue (eliminating subtle errors) but also harms surveyability if the detail is overwhelming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trustworthiness of the software/implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: The correctness of any computer-assisted proof depends on the trustworthiness of the software (code, SAT solvers, proof assistants) used to produce or check it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical anxieties (e.g., Appel–Haken’s reliance on an assembly program to check reducible configurations) show concern about bugs in code. Such worries are analogous to human error in hand proofs; the criterion requires examining plausibility of implementation errors and mitigation (formal verification of the tools, code review, independent re-checks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveyability vs size/importance tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a pragmatic tradeoff: enormous machine-generated proofs may be accepted despite being unsurveyable, especially when the claimed fact has limited wider impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: millionth digit of pi, largest known prime, enormous SAT-solver proofs (Boolean Pythagorean Triples, 200 terabytes), non-existence of a projective plane of order 10. If a colossal proof has major implications, discomfort rises; if it is peripheral, accepting it pragmatically may be reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to sample-check parts for confidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When full surveyability is impossible, being able to inspect small but arbitrary parts of a large proof can help establish confidence in its correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For colossal proofs produced by SAT solvers or large computations, checking arbitrary fragments or rerunning independent computations provides partial but useful assurance of correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community acceptance as pragmatic standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Pragmatically, mathematicians’ willingness to use and accept proof assistants is part of what determines whether machine proofs count as proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasises that mathematicians must adopt and trust proof assistants; acceptance by the community functions as a de facto standard even if individual members cannot read the full formalisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between empirical/numerical evidence and proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive numerical calculations or empirical evidence (e.g., computations supporting the Riemann hypothesis) are not substitutes for mathematical proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computational evidence may strongly suggest a fact but is not a proof; formal logical demonstration (or formalised computational proof) is required for mathematical certainty. This separates philosophical acceptance of computational results from outright proof.
